## Why R?

-   R is an impressive, do-it-all software: loading spatial datasets, to fitting models, analyzing patterns, and creating publication-quality maps and plots.
-   **reproducibility** of data summaries and statistical analyses.
-   **Automation**: automates repetitive or mundane data processing tasks.
-   **Open-source and free**: constant updates contributed by scientists worldwide.

::: notes
This introductory lab is a foundation for students who have not used R often, or who want to review the basics of data and spatial data structures. Everything in this deck runs in the browser, so nobody needs a working local install on day one.
:::

## Getting Help in R

-   To view documentation for any loaded function, use `help()` or `?`:

```{r}
?runif
help(runif)
```

-   `help(package = "sf")` lists every function in a package.
-   `??aggregate` runs a fuzzy search.
-   Online resources are enormous.

::: notes
In R you never have to memorise code. Help pages document the expected inputs (arguments) and the returned value. 
:::

# R Syntax and Objects

## Objects and Assignment

The core building block in R is the **object**. Objects hold data, models, and functions.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
# Assign a sequence of numbers to an object named x
x <- 1:15

# Display it
print(x)
```

::: callout-note
`<-` is the assignment arrow. Typing the object's name (or wrapping it in `print()`) displays its contents.
:::

## Objects Can Be Overwritten

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x <- 1 + 15     # x is overwritten
y <- 5.2        # second object
z <- x^y        # third object

z

ls()            # list every object in the workspace
```

> Notice that `x` now holds 16. The previous contents are gone without warning.

## Objects Hold Any Type

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x <- "wolverine"
y <- FALSE
z <- 42L

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
```

::: callout-note
Character values are wrapped in quotation marks. `TRUE` and `FALSE` are not, and must be uppercase. The `L` suffix forces an integer.
:::

## Vectors

A **vector** is a sequence of values of one type. Build one with `c()`.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg  <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)
species  <- c("wolverine", "black bear", "marten", "coyote")
mt_range <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

length(mass_kg)
mean(mass_kg)
species[2]              # second element
mass_kg[mass_kg > 30]   # logical subsetting
```

## Vectors

Math operations are done element by element and no loop is required.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)

mass_lb <- mass_kg * 2.205
round(mass_lb, 1)

# Summary statistics
c(min = min(mass_kg), max = max(mass_kg), sd = round(sd(mass_kg), 2))
```

## Data Frames

A **data frame** stitches vectors together as columns of a table. Columns may hold different types; every column must be the same length.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg  <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)
species  <- c("wolverine", "black bear", "marten", "coyote")
mt_range <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

sp_data <- data.frame(species, mass_kg, mt_range)
sp_data

str(sp_data)
```

## Your Turn: Classes and Subsetting

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1"}
Three transects were surveyed: North, Mid, and South and bird observations were counted along the transect. Run the code, then change the threshold from 10 to 15 and re-run. What does `subset()` give you when nothing matches?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
site_names <- c("North", "Mid", "South")
counts     <- c(12, 18, 5)
my_df      <- data.frame(site = site_names, count = counts)

my_df

# Keep only rows where count is greater than 10
sub_df <- subset(my_df, count > 10)
sub_df
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why no `my_df$`?"}
The '\[' below is more predictable than `subset()`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
sub_df <- subset(my_df, count > 10)          #<1>
sub_df

# The bracket equivalent, which is worth knowing:
my_df[my_df$count > 10, ]                    #<2>
```

1.  `subset()` evaluates the condition inside the data frame.
2.  Brackets take `[rows, columns]`; leaving the column slot empty keeps all columns.
:::

# Simulating and Exploring a Dataset

## Why Simulate?

-   Simulated data are **reproducible**
-   You know the **truth**, so you can check whether your analysis recovers it.

Every dataset in this lesson is generated by the code you can see. Nothing is loaded from disk or from the internet.

::: notes
This is also how you check whether an estimator is behaving: simulate from known parameters, fit the model, and see whether the estimates land near the truth.
:::

## Simulate a Camera-Trap Dataset

Run this cell before the ones that follow. The object `camera` is used on the next several slides.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)

sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")

camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week    = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$age   <- sample(c("Adult", "Juvenile"), nrow(camera), TRUE, c(0.75, 0.25))
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

dim(camera)
head(camera)
```

::: callout-note
`expand.grid()` builds every combination of site, week, and species: 20 × 8 × 5 = 800 rows.
:::

## Inspecting a Data Frame

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
-   Each **row** is one observation
-   Each **column** is one variable
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(camera)
tail(camera, 3)
```
:::
:::::

::: callout-tip
What do you expect `tail()` to return before you run it?
:::

## Dimensions and Names

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
dim(camera)      # rows, then columns
nrow(camera)
ncol(camera)
names(camera)    # column names
str(camera)      # structure: class of every column
```

> `dim()` returns the size of each dimension. `dimnames()` returns row and column names, which for a data frame means row numbers and column names.

## Three Ways to Access a Column

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(camera$count)          # by name, with $
head(camera[, "count"])     # by name, with brackets
head(camera[, 6])           # by position
```

::: callout-tip
R is case sensitive. `camera$Count` returns `NULL`, not an error.
:::

## Row Subsetting

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
camera[1:3, ]                                    # rows 1 to 3

birds <- camera[camera$class == "Bird", ]        # logical condition
dim(birds)

elk_wk1 <- camera[camera$species == "Elk" & camera$week == 1, ]
elk_wk1
```

## Quantitative Summaries

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mean(camera$count)
round(mean(camera$count), 2)
summary(camera$count)

# Class of each variable
class(camera$count)
class(camera$species)
```

::: callout-warning
Why does `mean(camera$species)` fail? Run it and read the warning carefully — it is one you will meet often.
:::

## Sort and Order

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(sort(camera$count, decreasing = TRUE))   # sorts the values

ord <- order(camera$count, decreasing = TRUE) # returns positions
head(camera[ord, ])                           # reorders whole rows
```

::: callout-note
`sort()` returns values. `order()` returns the positions that would sort those values, which is what you need to reorder an entire table.
:::

## Tallies with `table()`

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
table(camera$age)

# Combinations of two variables
table(camera$class, camera$age)

# Number of species per class
table(camera$class, camera$species)
```

## Summaries with `aggregate()`

`table()` counts rows. `aggregate()` summarises a variable *within* groups.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
# Mean count per age class
aggregate(count ~ age, data = camera, FUN = mean)

# Break it down further
aggregate(count ~ class + age, data = camera, FUN = mean)

# Total detections per species
aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = sum)
```

## Writing Your Own Function

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
detection_rate <- function(counts) {
  n_surveys <- length(counts)
  n_detect  <- sum(counts > 0)
  return(n_detect / n_surveys)
}

detection_rate(camera$count)

# Apply it by species
tapply(camera$count, camera$species, detection_rate)
```

::: callout-note
Saving functions in a separate script and calling `source("my_functions.R")` keeps analysis scripts readable.
:::

## Saving and Reloading

```{r, echo = TRUE}
write.csv(camera, "camera.csv", row.names = FALSE)
save(camera, file = "camera.RData")
#list.files()

rm(camera)                # remove from workspace
exists("camera")

load("camera.RData")      # bring it back
exists("camera")
head(camera, 3)
```

::: callout-note
`.RData` preserves classes and attributes exactly. `.csv` is portable but forgets that `week` was an integer and `class` was a character.
:::

## Your Turn: Explore the Data

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 2"}
Using the simulated `camera` data, answer the questions below:

1.  How many total detections were recorded across all rows?
2.  How many species had at least one detection?
3.  How many detections came from birds versus mammals?
4.  Which species had the highest mean count per survey?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$age   <- sample(c("Adult", "Juvenile"), nrow(camera), TRUE, c(0.75, 0.25))
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

# 1. Total detections
sum(camera$count)

# 2. Number of species with at least one detection
length(unique(camera$species[camera$count > 0]))

# 3. Detections by class
aggregate(count ~ class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

# 4. Mean count per species, highest first
mn <- aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = mean)
mn[order(mn$count, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
`sum()`, `unique()` with `length()`, `aggregate()`, and `order()` cover all four questions.

``` r
sum(camera$count)
length(unique(camera$species[camera$count > 0]))
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
# 1.
sum(camera$count)

# 2.
detected <- camera[camera$count > 0, ]
length(unique(detected$species))

# 3.
aggregate(count ~ class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

# 4.
mn <- aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = mean)
mn[order(mn$count, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
:::

# Random Sampling and Distributions

## What Is Randomness?

-   Every element has an **equal and independent** chance of being selected.
-   We cannot predict any single outcome with certainty — this is a **random (stochastic)** process.
-   Humans are poor random number generators. Ask ten people for "30 random points" and you will get suspiciously even spacing. That is why we use algorithms.

## Uniform Distribution

Start with 100 draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 10.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

summary(x_unif)
plot(x_unif, type = "h", col = "#333333",
     xlab = "Draw number", ylab = "Value",
     main = "100 uniform draws in the order sampled")
```

> Compare your output with your neighbour's. Did you get the same values?

## Reproducibility with `set.seed()`

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
a <- runif(5, 0, 10)

set.seed(2026)
b <- runif(5, 0, 10)

round(a, 4)
round(b, 4)
identical(a, b)
```

::: callout-note
`set.seed()` fixes the starting point of the random number generator. Put it at the top of any script you want to be reproducible.
:::

## Visualising the Distribution

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

hist(x_unif,
     col    = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab   = "Value",
     main   = "Uniform(0, 10), n = 100")
```

The bars are roughly level across the range because every value between 0 and 10 is equally likely. With only 100 draws the sampling noise is still obvious.

## Sample Size and Shape

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 3"}
Run the code, then change the four sample sizes and re-run. How does the histogram shape change as `n` grows?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

As `n` grows the bars flatten out toward the true uniform density. Small samples look lumpy purely by chance — a useful reminder when you interpret a histogram of 30 field measurements.
:::

## Normal Distribution

`rnorm()` takes a sample size, a mean, and a standard deviation.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

summary(x_norm)
round(c(mean = mean(x_norm), sd = sd(x_norm)), 3)
```

> Are the sample mean and standard deviation exactly 0 and 1? Why not?

## Density, Mean, and Interval

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

plot(density(x_norm),
     lwd = 3,
     col = "#333333",
     main = "Normal(0, 1),
     n = 100",
     xlab = "Value")

abline(v = mean(x_norm), lwd = 3, col = "#70002E")

ci <- quantile(x_norm, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v = ci, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#70002E")

legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Density", "Mean", "95% interval"),
       col = c("#333333", "#70002E", "#70002E"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       lwd = c(3, 3, 2))
```

The solid maroon line marks the sample mean near zero; the dashed lines mark the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, roughly symmetric around it.

## Histogram and Density Together

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

hist(x_norm, 
     probability = TRUE,
     col = "#EFE8D4",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Value", 
     main = "")
lines(density(x_norm), col = "#70002E", lwd = 4)
```

::: callout-note
`probability = TRUE` plots density rather than frequency, so the histogram and the smooth curve share a vertical scale. With `probability = FALSE` (the default) the curve would be flat against the axis.
:::

## Comparing Two Distributions

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
x1 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 25, sd = 5)   # adults
x2 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 15, sd = 2)   # juveniles

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(density(x1),
     col = "#70002E",
     lwd = 4,
     lty = 1,
     xlim = c(5, 45), 
     ylim = c(0, 0.30),
     main = "Kernel densities", 
     xlab = "Mass (kg)")
lines(density(x2), col = "#1D3C34", lwd = 4, lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Adult", "Juvenile"),
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"),
       lty = c(1, 2),
       lwd = 4)

mass <- rbind(data.frame(x = x1, stage = "Adult"),
              data.frame(x = x2, stage = "Juvenile"))
boxplot(x ~ stage, 
        data = mass, 
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#BBDDE6"),
        ylab = "Mass (kg)",
        xlab = "",
        main = "Box-and-whisker")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Adults centre near 25 kg with a wide spread; juveniles centre near 15 kg and are much tighter. Line type distinguishes the two curves as well as colour.

## Poisson Distribution

Count data are often modelled as Poisson. It has a single parameter, the mean count λ (lambda).

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
x_pois <- rpois(n = 250, lambda = 3.3)

table(x_pois)
hist(x_pois, 
     probability = TRUE,
     breaks = seq(-0.5, max(x_pois) + 0.5, 1),
     col = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Count", 
     main = "Poisson(lambda = 3.3)")
```

::: callout-note
For a Poisson, the variance equals the mean. Real count data are often **overdispersed**, i.e., more variable and that is when negative binomial models are useful.
:::

## Your Turn: Three Values of Lambda

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 4"}
Run the code, then change the three values of λ. At what point does the distribution stop looking skewed?
:::

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
       main = paste("lambda =", m),
       xlab = "Count",
       probability = TRUE,
       col = "#DFD1A7",
       border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
  main = paste("lambda =", m),
  xlab = "Count",
  probability = TRUE, 
  col = "#DFD1A7", 
  border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

At λ = 1 the distribution is strongly right-skewed and piles up at zero. By λ = 15 it is nearly symmetric — Poisson approaches normal as λ grows.
:::

## Binomial and Bernoulli

The binomial arises when repeated trials have binary outcome. `rbinom()` takes the number of observations, trials per observation, and probability of success.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)

# 10 observations, each of 5 trials, p = 0.25
x_binom <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.25)
x_binom

# Bernoulli: a single trial per observation
x_bern <- rbinom(n = 20, size = 1, prob = 0.35)
x_bern

barplot(table(factor(x_bern, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Failure", "Success"))),
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#70002E"),
        xlab = "Outcome", ylab = "Number of cases")
```

::: callout-note
This is the detection process behind occupancy models: each camera visit is a Bernoulli trial with detection probability *p*, and the number of visits with a detection out of *K* visits is binomial.
:::

# Graphics in R

## Base Plotting Functions

-   `plot(x, y)` : scatter, line, or formula plots
-   `hist(x)` : distribution of one variable
-   `boxplot(y ~ group)` : distribution across groups
-   `barplot(height)` : tallies and totals
-   `pairs(df)` : all pairwise scatterplots, for spotting collinearity among predictors

Add-on packages include `ggplot2` and `lattice`. We use base graphics here because `terra` and `sf` both plug straight into it.

## A First Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera),
                      lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))
wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)
wk

plot(count ~ week, data = wk)
```

The default plot is functional but can be customized, shown next.

## Controlling the Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)

plot(count ~ week,
     data = wk,
     type  = "l", lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#767676",
     axes  = FALSE, frame = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(0.5, 8.5),
     ylim  = c(0, max(wk$count) + 40),
     xaxs  = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab  = "Survey week",
     ylab  = "Total detections")

axis(1, at = 1:8, labels = 1:8, las = 1, lwd = 2)
axis(2, at = seq(0, max(wk$count) + 40, 40), las = 1, lwd = 2)

points(count ~ week, data = wk, pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = "#70002E")
```

Detections stay roughly the same across the eight weeks, as they should. The simulation used the same λ every week.

## Two Groups on One Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
wk_cls <- aggregate(count ~ week + class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

mam <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Mammal", ]
avs <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Bird", ]

plot(count ~ week, data = mam,
     pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = "#70002E", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 1,
     ylim = c(0, max(wk_cls$count) + 20),
     xlab = "Survey week", ylab = "Total detections")

points(count ~ week, data = avs,
       pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = "#1D3C34", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Mammals", "Birds"),
       pch = c(19, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2,
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Design note"}
The two series differ by **colour, point shape, and line type**. Redundant encoding keeps the figure readable in greyscale and for colour-blind readers.
:::

## Bar Plots of Totals

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
tot <- tapply(camera$count, camera$species, sum)
tot <- sort(tot, decreasing = TRUE)

par(mar = c(9, 5, 2, 1))
barplot(tot,
        col       = "#70002E",
        density   = seq(20, 60, length.out = length(tot)),
        ylab      = "Total detections",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.9)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

## Small Multiples

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
sp_list <- unique(camera$species)
wk_sp   <- aggregate(count ~ week + species, data = camera, FUN = sum)

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (s in sp_list) {
  d <- wk_sp[wk_sp$species == s, ]
  plot(count ~ week, data = d,
       type = "h", lwd = 8, lend = 1, col = "#1D3C34",
       ylim = c(0, max(wk_sp$count)),
       main = s, cex.main = 0.95,
       xlab = "Week", ylab = "Detections")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

Shared axis limits across panels are what make small multiples comparable. Drop `ylim` and each panel rescales, which hides the real differences between species.

Run the code, then swap `class` for `species` in the formula. You will need `las = 2` to keep the labels readable.
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp, 
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

boxplot(count ~ class, data = camera,
        col  = c("#BBDDE6", "#DFD1A7"),
        xlab = "Class",
        ylab = "Detections per survey")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The formula reads *response* `~` *grouping variable*. The response is what you measured; the grouping variable is what splits the boxes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
boxplot(count ~ class, 
        data = camera,
        col  = c("#BBDDE6", "#DFD1A7"),
        xlab = "Class",
        ylab = "Detections per survey")
```

Birds sit higher because the simulation used λ = 2.5 for birds and λ = 1.2 for mammals.
:::

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

# Introduction

## Why R?

-   R is an impressive, do-it-all software: loading spatial datasets, to fitting models, analyzing patterns, and creating publication-quality maps and plots.
-   **reproducibility** of data summaries and statistical analyses.
-   **Automation**: automates repetitive or mundane data processing tasks.
-   **Open-source and free**: constant updates contributed by scientists worldwide.

::: notes
This introductory lab is a foundation for students who have not used R often, or who want to review the basics of data and spatial data structures. Everything in this deck runs in the browser, so nobody needs a working local install on day one.
:::

## Getting Help in R

-   To view documentation for any loaded function, use `help()` or `?`:

```{r}
?runif
help(runif)
```

-   `help(package = "sf")` lists every function in a package.
-   `??aggregate` runs a fuzzy search.
-   Online resources are enormous.

::: notes
In R you never have to memorise code. Help pages document the expected inputs (arguments) and the returned value. 
:::

# R Syntax and Objects

## Objects and Assignment

The core building block in R is the **object**. Objects hold data, models, and functions.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
# Assign a sequence of numbers to an object named x
x <- 1:15

# Display it
print(x)
```

::: callout-note
`<-` is the assignment arrow. Typing the object's name (or wrapping it in `print()`) displays its contents.
:::

## Objects Can Be Overwritten

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x <- 1 + 15     # x is overwritten
y <- 5.2        # second object
z <- x^y        # third object

z

ls()            # list every object in the workspace
```

> Notice that `x` now holds 16. The previous contents are gone without warning.

## Objects Hold Any Type

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x <- "wolverine"
y <- FALSE
z <- 42L

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
```

::: callout-note
Character values are wrapped in quotation marks. `TRUE` and `FALSE` are not, and must be uppercase. The `L` suffix forces an integer.
:::

## Vectors

A **vector** is a sequence of values of one type. Build one with `c()`.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg  <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)
species  <- c("wolverine", "black bear", "marten", "coyote")
mt_range <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

length(mass_kg)
mean(mass_kg)
species[2]              # second element
mass_kg[mass_kg > 30]   # logical subsetting
```

## Vectors

Math operations are done element by element and no loop is required.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)

mass_lb <- mass_kg * 2.205
round(mass_lb, 1)

# Summary statistics
c(min = min(mass_kg), max = max(mass_kg), sd = round(sd(mass_kg), 2))
```

## Data Frames

A **data frame** stitches vectors together as columns of a table. Columns may hold different types; every column must be the same length.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mass_kg  <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)
species  <- c("wolverine", "black bear", "marten", "coyote")
mt_range <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

sp_data <- data.frame(species, mass_kg, mt_range)
sp_data

str(sp_data)
```

## Your Turn: Classes and Subsetting

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1"}
Three transects were surveyed: North, Mid, and South and bird observations were counted along the transect. Run the code, then change the threshold from 10 to 15 and re-run. What does `subset()` give you when nothing matches?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
site_names <- c("North", "Mid", "South")
counts     <- c(12, 18, 5)
my_df      <- data.frame(site = site_names, count = counts)

my_df

# Keep only rows where count is greater than 10
sub_df <- subset(my_df, count > 10)
sub_df
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why no `my_df$`?"}
The '\[' below is more predictable than `subset()`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
sub_df <- subset(my_df, count > 10)          #<1>
sub_df

# The bracket equivalent, which is worth knowing:
my_df[my_df$count > 10, ]                    #<2>
```

1.  `subset()` evaluates the condition inside the data frame.
2.  Brackets take `[rows, columns]`; leaving the column slot empty keeps all columns.
:::

# Simulating and Exploring a Dataset

## Why Simulate?

-   Simulated data are **reproducible**
-   You know the **truth**, so you can check whether your analysis recovers it.

Every dataset in this lesson is generated by the code you can see. Nothing is loaded from disk or from the internet.

::: notes
This is also how you check whether an estimator is behaving: simulate from known parameters, fit the model, and see whether the estimates land near the truth.
:::

## Simulate a Camera-Trap Dataset

Run this cell before the ones that follow. The object `camera` is used on the next several slides.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)

sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")

camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week    = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$age   <- sample(c("Adult", "Juvenile"), nrow(camera), TRUE, c(0.75, 0.25))
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

dim(camera)
head(camera)
```

::: callout-note
`expand.grid()` builds every combination of site, week, and species: 20 × 8 × 5 = 800 rows.
:::

## Inspecting a Data Frame

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
-   Each **row** is one observation
-   Each **column** is one variable
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(camera)
tail(camera, 3)
```
:::
:::::

::: callout-tip
What do you expect `tail()` to return before you run it?
:::

## Dimensions and Names

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
dim(camera)      # rows, then columns
nrow(camera)
ncol(camera)
names(camera)    # column names
str(camera)      # structure: class of every column
```

> `dim()` returns the size of each dimension. `dimnames()` returns row and column names, which for a data frame means row numbers and column names.

## Three Ways to Access a Column

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(camera$count)          # by name, with $
head(camera[, "count"])     # by name, with brackets
head(camera[, 6])           # by position
```

::: callout-tip
R is case sensitive. `camera$Count` returns `NULL`, not an error.
:::

## Row Subsetting

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
camera[1:3, ]                                    # rows 1 to 3

birds <- camera[camera$class == "Bird", ]        # logical condition
dim(birds)

elk_wk1 <- camera[camera$species == "Elk" & camera$week == 1, ]
elk_wk1
```

## Quantitative Summaries

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
mean(camera$count)
round(mean(camera$count), 2)
summary(camera$count)

# Class of each variable
class(camera$count)
class(camera$species)
```

::: callout-warning
Why does `mean(camera$species)` fail? Run it and read the warning carefully — it is one you will meet often.
:::

## Sort and Order

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
head(sort(camera$count, decreasing = TRUE))   # sorts the values

ord <- order(camera$count, decreasing = TRUE) # returns positions
head(camera[ord, ])                           # reorders whole rows
```

::: callout-note
`sort()` returns values. `order()` returns the positions that would sort those values, which is what you need to reorder an entire table.
:::

## Tallies with `table()`

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
table(camera$age)

# Combinations of two variables
table(camera$class, camera$age)

# Number of species per class
table(camera$class, camera$species)
```

## Summaries with `aggregate()`

`table()` counts rows. `aggregate()` summarises a variable *within* groups.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
# Mean count per age class
aggregate(count ~ age, data = camera, FUN = mean)

# Break it down further
aggregate(count ~ class + age, data = camera, FUN = mean)

# Total detections per species
aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = sum)
```

## Writing Your Own Function

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
detection_rate <- function(counts) {
  n_surveys <- length(counts)
  n_detect  <- sum(counts > 0)
  return(n_detect / n_surveys)
}

detection_rate(camera$count)

# Apply it by species
tapply(camera$count, camera$species, detection_rate)
```

::: callout-note
Saving functions in a separate script and calling `source("my_functions.R")` keeps analysis scripts readable.
:::

## Saving and Reloading

```{r, echo = TRUE}
write.csv(camera, "camera.csv", row.names = FALSE)
save(camera, file = "camera.RData")
#list.files()

rm(camera)                # remove from workspace
exists("camera")

load("camera.RData")      # bring it back
exists("camera")
head(camera, 3)
```

::: callout-note
`.RData` preserves classes and attributes exactly. `.csv` is portable but forgets that `week` was an integer and `class` was a character.
:::

## Your Turn: Explore the Data

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 2"}
Using the simulated `camera` data, answer the questions below:

1.  How many total detections were recorded across all rows?
2.  How many species had at least one detection?
3.  How many detections came from birds versus mammals?
4.  Which species had the highest mean count per survey?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$age   <- sample(c("Adult", "Juvenile"), nrow(camera), TRUE, c(0.75, 0.25))
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

# 1. Total detections
sum(camera$count)

# 2. Number of species with at least one detection
length(unique(camera$species[camera$count > 0]))

# 3. Detections by class
aggregate(count ~ class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

# 4. Mean count per species, highest first
mn <- aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = mean)
mn[order(mn$count, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
`sum()`, `unique()` with `length()`, `aggregate()`, and `order()` cover all four questions.

``` r
sum(camera$count)
length(unique(camera$species[camera$count > 0]))
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
# 1.
sum(camera$count)

# 2.
detected <- camera[camera$count > 0, ]
length(unique(detected$species))

# 3.
aggregate(count ~ class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

# 4.
mn <- aggregate(count ~ species, data = camera, FUN = mean)
mn[order(mn$count, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
:::

# Random Sampling and Distributions

## What Is Randomness?

-   Every element has an **equal and independent** chance of being selected.
-   We cannot predict any single outcome with certainty — this is a **random (stochastic)** process.
-   Humans are poor random number generators. Ask ten people for "30 random points" and you will get suspiciously even spacing. That is why we use algorithms.

## Uniform Distribution

Start with 100 draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 10.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

summary(x_unif)
plot(x_unif, type = "h", col = "#333333",
     xlab = "Draw number", ylab = "Value",
     main = "100 uniform draws in the order sampled")
```

> Compare your output with your neighbour's. Did you get the same values?

## Reproducibility with `set.seed()`

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
a <- runif(5, 0, 10)

set.seed(2026)
b <- runif(5, 0, 10)

round(a, 4)
round(b, 4)
identical(a, b)
```

::: callout-note
`set.seed()` fixes the starting point of the random number generator. Put it at the top of any script you want to be reproducible.
:::

## Visualising the Distribution

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

hist(x_unif,
     col    = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab   = "Value",
     main   = "Uniform(0, 10), n = 100")
```

The bars are roughly level across the range because every value between 0 and 10 is equally likely. With only 100 draws the sampling noise is still obvious.

## Sample Size and Shape

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 3"}
Run the code, then change the four sample sizes and re-run. How does the histogram shape change as `n` grows?
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

As `n` grows the bars flatten out toward the true uniform density. Small samples look lumpy purely by chance — a useful reminder when you interpret a histogram of 30 field measurements.
:::

## Normal Distribution

`rnorm()` takes a sample size, a mean, and a standard deviation.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

summary(x_norm)
round(c(mean = mean(x_norm), sd = sd(x_norm)), 3)
```

> Are the sample mean and standard deviation exactly 0 and 1? Why not?

## Density, Mean, and Interval

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

plot(density(x_norm),
     lwd = 3,
     col = "#333333",
     main = "Normal(0, 1),
     n = 100",
     xlab = "Value")

abline(v = mean(x_norm), lwd = 3, col = "#70002E")

ci <- quantile(x_norm, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v = ci, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#70002E")

legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Density", "Mean", "95% interval"),
       col = c("#333333", "#70002E", "#70002E"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       lwd = c(3, 3, 2))
```

The solid maroon line marks the sample mean near zero; the dashed lines mark the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, roughly symmetric around it.

## Histogram and Density Together

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

hist(x_norm, 
     probability = TRUE,
     col = "#EFE8D4",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Value", 
     main = "")
lines(density(x_norm), col = "#70002E", lwd = 4)
```

::: callout-note
`probability = TRUE` plots density rather than frequency, so the histogram and the smooth curve share a vertical scale. With `probability = FALSE` (the default) the curve would be flat against the axis.
:::

## Comparing Two Distributions

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
x1 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 25, sd = 5)   # adults
x2 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 15, sd = 2)   # juveniles

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(density(x1),
     col = "#70002E",
     lwd = 4,
     lty = 1,
     xlim = c(5, 45), 
     ylim = c(0, 0.30),
     main = "Kernel densities", 
     xlab = "Mass (kg)")
lines(density(x2), col = "#1D3C34", lwd = 4, lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Adult", "Juvenile"),
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"),
       lty = c(1, 2),
       lwd = 4)

mass <- rbind(data.frame(x = x1, stage = "Adult"),
              data.frame(x = x2, stage = "Juvenile"))
boxplot(x ~ stage, 
        data = mass, 
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#BBDDE6"),
        ylab = "Mass (kg)",
        xlab = "",
        main = "Box-and-whisker")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Adults centre near 25 kg with a wide spread; juveniles centre near 15 kg and are much tighter. Line type distinguishes the two curves as well as colour.

## Poisson Distribution

Count data are often modelled as Poisson. It has a single parameter, the mean count λ (lambda).

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
x_pois <- rpois(n = 250, lambda = 3.3)

table(x_pois)
hist(x_pois, 
     probability = TRUE,
     breaks = seq(-0.5, max(x_pois) + 0.5, 1),
     col = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Count", 
     main = "Poisson(lambda = 3.3)")
```

::: callout-note
For a Poisson, the variance equals the mean. Real count data are often **overdispersed**, i.e., more variable and that is when negative binomial models are useful.
:::

## Your Turn: Three Values of Lambda

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 4"}
Run the code, then change the three values of λ. At what point does the distribution stop looking skewed?
:::

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
       main = paste("lambda =", m),
       xlab = "Count",
       probability = TRUE,
       col = "#DFD1A7",
       border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
  main = paste("lambda =", m),
  xlab = "Count",
  probability = TRUE, 
  col = "#DFD1A7", 
  border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

At λ = 1 the distribution is strongly right-skewed and piles up at zero. By λ = 15 it is nearly symmetric — Poisson approaches normal as λ grows.
:::

## Binomial and Bernoulli

The binomial arises when repeated trials have binary outcome. `rbinom()` takes the number of observations, trials per observation, and probability of success.

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)

# 10 observations, each of 5 trials, p = 0.25
x_binom <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.25)
x_binom

# Bernoulli: a single trial per observation
x_bern <- rbinom(n = 20, size = 1, prob = 0.35)
x_bern

barplot(table(factor(x_bern, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Failure", "Success"))),
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#70002E"),
        xlab = "Outcome", ylab = "Number of cases")
```

::: callout-note
This is the detection process behind occupancy models: each camera visit is a Bernoulli trial with detection probability *p*, and the number of visits with a detection out of *K* visits is binomial.
:::

# Graphics in R

## Base Plotting Functions

-   `plot(x, y)` : scatter, line, or formula plots
-   `hist(x)` : distribution of one variable
-   `boxplot(y ~ group)` : distribution across groups
-   `barplot(height)` : tallies and totals
-   `pairs(df)` : all pairwise scatterplots, for spotting collinearity among predictors

Add-on packages include `ggplot2` and `lattice`. We use base graphics here because `terra` and `sf` both plug straight into it.

## A First Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera),
                      lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))
wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)
wk

plot(count ~ week, data = wk)
```

The default plot is functional but can be customized, shown next.

## Controlling the Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)

plot(count ~ week,
     data = wk,
     type  = "l", lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#767676",
     axes  = FALSE, frame = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(0.5, 8.5),
     ylim  = c(0, max(wk$count) + 40),
     xaxs  = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab  = "Survey week",
     ylab  = "Total detections")

axis(1, at = 1:8, labels = 1:8, las = 1, lwd = 2)
axis(2, at = seq(0, max(wk$count) + 40, 40), las = 1, lwd = 2)

points(count ~ week, data = wk, pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = "#70002E")
```

Detections stay roughly the same across the eight weeks, as they should. The simulation used the same λ every week.

## Two Groups on One Plot

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
wk_cls <- aggregate(count ~ week + class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

mam <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Mammal", ]
avs <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Bird", ]

plot(count ~ week, data = mam,
     pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = "#70002E", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 1,
     ylim = c(0, max(wk_cls$count) + 20),
     xlab = "Survey week", ylab = "Total detections")

points(count ~ week, data = avs,
       pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = "#1D3C34", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Mammals", "Birds"),
       pch = c(19, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2,
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Design note"}
The two series differ by **colour, point shape, and line type**. Redundant encoding keeps the figure readable in greyscale and for colour-blind readers.
:::

## Bar Plots of Totals

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
tot <- tapply(camera$count, camera$species, sum)
tot <- sort(tot, decreasing = TRUE)

par(mar = c(9, 5, 2, 1))
barplot(tot,
        col       = "#70002E",
        density   = seq(20, 60, length.out = length(tot)),
        ylab      = "Total detections",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.9)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

## Small Multiples

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
sp_list <- unique(camera$species)
wk_sp   <- aggregate(count ~ week + species, data = camera, FUN = sum)

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (s in sp_list) {
  d <- wk_sp[wk_sp$species == s, ]
  plot(count ~ week, data = d,
       type = "h", lwd = 8, lend = 1, col = "#1D3C34",
       ylim = c(0, max(wk_sp$count)),
       main = s, cex.main = 0.95,
       xlab = "Week", ylab = "Detections")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

Shared axis limits across panels are what make small multiples comparable. Drop `ylim` and each panel rescales, which hides the real differences between species.

## Your Turn: Build a Figure

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 5"}
Run the code, then swap `class` for `species` in the formula. You will need `las = 2` to keep the labels readable.
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, inlude = TRUE}
set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp, 
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera), lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))

boxplot(count ~ class, data = camera,
        col  = c("#BBDDE6", "#DFD1A7"),
        xlab = "Class",
        ylab = "Detections per survey")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The formula reads *response* `~` *grouping variable*. The response is what you measured; the grouping variable is what splits the boxes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
boxplot(count ~ class, 
        data = camera,
        col  = c("#BBDDE6", "#DFD1A7"),
        xlab = "Class",
        ylab = "Detections per survey")
```

Birds sit higher because the simulation used λ = 2.5 for birds and λ = 1.2 for mammals.
